questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: Ireland is the only EU country where everything is in English. University College Dublin allowed me to choose a wide range of modules rather than sticking to a single course, which was very appealing to me as a nanoscience student. Dublin is a nice city with loads of pubs, and Ireland is a beautiful country with infinitely many hikes and sheep!

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: UCD offered a reception open 24-7 for enquiries about accommodation etc. A lot of information had been sent out per email, so information was generally well distributed, and the local Erasmus office was very responsive at the beginning of my stay.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Check-in to my on-campus accommodation, a few info meetings on zoom which were, however, not very helpful.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: A range of rooms in dorms ranging from 4-16 people. The price range was approximately €900-€1500 per month

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: One of the most expensive had food (read: fries) included. All accommodation had kitchens available, even though a rent of €1250 per month was not enough to have access to an oven...

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: It is grand, as they say in Ireland. The facilities are generally fine, but of course the more expensive dorms have nicer facilities. Mainly exchange students live on campus because it is crazy expensive, but it is not much cheaper to live outside of campus, so most Irish people live at home. As such, I don't think is is worth the effort to look for slightly cheaper accommodation in the city, unless you specifically want to live in the city center. The social life with other exchange students is also much easier when you live on campus.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It was sooo expensive, and I think UCD took advantage of their many exchange students by continually increasing the rent. People who only stay for 4-8 months are more inclined to power through and pay the sky-high prices.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: There seemed to be no general coordination of timetables across different modules. Choosing modules from different courses was very difficult since they often overlapped and it was not allowed to have even a single timetable crash. I had pre-approval for 17 different modules, but I could not combine them in a way that made sense while not having any overlaps, and I must have written back and forth 10 times before I got registered. On the other hand, many of these difficulties stemmed from the fact that I was able to pick courses from different schools, which was ultimately a nice oppertunity.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You have to manually look up the random time-slots for every module you consider taking and make sure there are no timetable clashes. The registration is done manually by sending an email with all your desired module names. You are able to change your modules during the first three weeks of lectures, which is awesome!

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Email interaction with a coordinator.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I ended up registering for 5/6 modules I was interested in. For my final class I had to register for a module with classes in the evening to avoid timetable clashes. The module was bad, but I met a couple of nice people there, so i guess it was worth it.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: If you are not following a specific course (e.g. chemistry, physics or whatever they have) it can be very difficult to make the timetable work. I made several draft-timetables in excel by plugging in the times from their course catalogue, but I still had to compromise on my desired modules.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I generally had one third good modules, one third easy modules and one third poorly taught modules. For me, the easy modules freed time to have fun and travel, while the poorly taught ones offered an opportunity to dive into the topics when doing the big assignments by myself, and the good modules kept me afloat when I was about to lose motivation.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: There was no hands-on lab experiences, only in the form of data treatment and computer work. Other than that the style was very comparable but he execution often left much to be desired.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
English for Academic Writing 5, 
Data Science in Python, 
Nanomaterials Chemistry, 
Chem Proc Sust & Ren Energy, 
Advanced Characterisation Tech, 
Advanced Topics in Computational Science

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Advanced Topics in Computational Science: The lecturer is very enthusiastic and competent, and you get to code up some cool models without a lot of prior experience. All around good craic!

(Data Science in Python): A good introduction to working in python if you, like me, could not find that at UCPH. The module is not very inspiring but I think I learned a lot of useful skills.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Nothing major, but going to bars, weekend trips etc. turned out to be essential and expensive in the long run.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Buying food (not cooking) was expensive. Accommodation was expensive. Public transport for students was cheap.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: There are ~100 different clubs and societies, so go crazy!

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: All sports you can mention as well as other societies including ones for different cultures (german, indian, french etc.), food, games, you name it.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: The mountaineering club do climbing classes twice a week, a hiking trip every Sunday, and occasionally longer trips, check it out! The "res-life" (people living on-campus) arrange football every week as wel as events such as dating shows, talents shows, super bowl nights etc, it's nice. The Clubhouse (the student bar) have four events a week including pub quiz, music quiz and karaoke.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Go to everywhere in Ireland. All of the five biggest cities are well worth a trip, and I'm sure plenty of the smaller ones are too! Train tickets across the country are crazy cheap (~100DKK), but you have to be 25 to rent a car (or check out GoCar, getting very specific). There are beautiful hikes in all kinds of terrains where ever you go, even the smallest village has at least one cozy pub and around Easter there are lambs everywhere, it's wild!

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: The Irish culture is not too different from the Danish one in a lot of ways, although they like them their rules, so they might throw your friends out of your apartment at 11pm on a Saturday or fine you €50 if your phone makes a sound during the exam. But don't we all love and respect authorities anyway?

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Nope, I found it very difficult to make Irish friends. I guess don't be afraid to go talk to people and do it every time you see them, because they will probably not seek you out actively.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Nothing really

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The open mindedness of people. Even though I found it hard to make real friends with the Irish, people are generally very welcoming and will chat you up in the pub or where ever you go.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
The on-campus accommodation is very expensive, but not that much more expensive than the rest of Dublin. If you can afford it, it is nice to live close to all the other exchange students in the everyday.
It is probably difficult to get exactly the modules you want to register for. However, my favorite modules ended up being completely different from what I thought, so don't worry too much about it.
There is a lot of continuous assessment rather than final exams. I ended up having one essay and one exam in the exam week even though I followed six modules.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: There is a pub close by called the Goat. It is located in Goatstown, has several bronze goat statues AND a couple of real goats living outside. Go here.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Meeting new friends from all over the world so I know where to travel the next 10 years :))

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: All the preparation: Filling in paperwork, applying foundations for money, registering for modules, registering for accommodation, finishing exams before leaving etc. But it was all worth it in the end!

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
